sections.title: 1. Mood and Affect

blocks.text: The terms affective disorder and mood disorder are used interchangeably in clinical practice. Mood refers to a more pervasive emotional state than affect (climate = mood, weather = affect). Both can have objective and subjective components, though one school uses mood for the subjective and affect for the objective components of emotional expression.

blocks.title: Aspects of affect
rows: The quality of affect: i.e. happy, depressed, perplexed, anxious or angry

Responsiveness of affect to environmental cues (we laugh on hearing a joke, blush when embarrassed). If reactivity is conspicuously absent this is called blunted affect or parathymia, according to Bleuler, who proposed it as a primary schizophrenic symptom
May be restricted or constricted in depression and anxiety states
Incongruent affect may be seen in hebephrenic schizophrenia and learning disability (e.g. a silly, jocular affect despite receiving bad news)

Reasonable maintenance of an affective state until a clear external stimulus demands change. Absence = labile affect (sudden unprovoked change, e.g. tears for no reason), seen in histrionic personality, borderline personality and sometimes post-traumatic stress disorder

An extreme form of labile affect is emotional incontinence, seen in organic states such as pseudobulbar palsy where the frontal lobe is damaged: bursts of laughter or tears within minutes with no control

blocks.text: Flattening of affect is keyed by unchanging facial expression, decreased spontaneous movements, poor eye contact and affective non-responsivity - **NOT** lability, incongruity, reactive affect or blunting, which sit beside it as look-alike options; the explanation defines it as diminution of the normal range of emotional experience and a negative symptom of schizophrenia.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/5) Descriptive Psychopathology Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Mania is characterised by extreme euphoria (disturbed emotion), pressured speech (disturbed thought) and too many ideas and plans to be carried out (disturbed will), so it is not a pure mood disorder. Euphoria, ecstasy and expansiveness refer to degrees of elevated mood without a thought or will component. 'Depression' in the clinical sense likewise includes mood, will and thought components, not just sad affect.

Melancholia is probably the oldest term in psychopathology: a quality of mood distinct from grief, occurring with significant psychomotor retardation, often with somatic symptoms of depression (as described in International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision). Patients describe it as a deeply distressing affective state.

bullets.text: Mood is the more pervasive emotional state (climate); affect is the momentary one (weather).
Six aspects of affect: valence, reactivity, range of expression, congruence, stability, control.
Absent reactivity = blunted affect / parathymia (Bleuler: a primary schizophrenic symptom); incongruent affect in hebephrenic schizophrenia and learning disability.

Labile affect: histrionic and borderline personality, sometimes post-traumatic stress disorder; its extreme form, emotional incontinence, occurs in organic states such as pseudobulbar palsy (frontal lobe damage).
Mania = disturbed emotion + thought (pressured speech) + will (too many plans); depression likewise includes mood, will and thought components.
Melancholia: a mood quality distinct from grief, with marked psychomotor retardation and often somatic symptoms (International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision).

sections.title: 2. Mood and Affect: mixed states, pain, anhedonia, alexithymia, time and age

blocks.text: Between the extremes of mania and depression various mixed states exist; according to recent literature, mixed states are commoner than pure mania or depression.

Over the years the six Kraepelinian mixed states have dwindled into two varieties: (1) Dysphoric Mania (predominant mania with some depressive symptoms) and (2) Depressive Mixed State (full depression with some manic symptoms).

'Depression with poverty of thought' is the option that is **NOT** a mixed affective state - the explanation says mixed states show incongruity between motor features and mood (mania with inhibition, depression with excitation); depressive mania, inhibited mania, excited/agitated depression and manic stupor are the other options offered.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/5) Descriptive Psychopathology Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Agitated depression (full depression with psychomotor agitation), anxious depression (marked anxiety), irritable depression (marked irritability) and mixed hypomania (hypomania with some depressive symptoms) are used in this context but are better avoided.

Pain is frequently associated with mood disturbances, and it is difficult to distinguish organic from non-organic pain because a pain syndrome often has mixed elements of both; nevertheless certain differences exist.

blocks.title: Organic vs non-organic pain
rows: Often fluctuant and remits during intervals
Progression, if it occurs, will have tissue boundaries
Head and neck, back are the most common
May have typical postural changes, e.g. intracranial pathology

blocks.text: For somatoform pain, head and neck are the most common sites. In somatisation disorder, musculoskeletal symptoms are the commonest; in hypochondriasis gastrointestinal symptoms predominate.

Anhedonia was coined by Ribot: inability to derive pleasure in life, often leading to diminished interests. Physical anhedonia is a defect in experiencing physical pleasures (eating, touching); social anhedonia is a defect in experiencing interpersonal pleasure (being with people, talking). It is a core symptom of melancholic depression with somatic syndrome, and part of the negative syndrome of schizophrenia, where it is considered more social/interpersonal than personal/physical.

Alexithymia was first described by Sifneos: A (absence/defective) + LEXI (words) + THYMIA (emotion), i.e. difficulties in using words to express emotions. It is often accompanied by (1) diminution of fantasy, (2) reduced symbolic thinking, (3) literal thinking concerned with details, (4) difficulties in recognising one's own feelings, (5) difficulties in differentiating body sensations and emotional states, (6) a 'robot-like existence' (though patients rarely complain in these terms).

Alexithymia is especially seen in psychosomatic illnesses, somatoform disorders, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, personality disorders and paraphilias. In some cultures, especially south Asian, somatic metaphors are often used in describing emotions.

Alexithymia is the tempting distractor in a 'which is **NOT** a negative symptom of schizophrenia' question - the listed negative symptoms are affective flattening or blunting, attentional impairment, avolition-apathy, anhedonia, asociality and alogia.

blocks.text: Mood and perception of time (Bschor et al. 2004; 32 acutely depressed, 30 acutely manic, 31 controls): the experience of time was assessed subjectively with a visual analogue scale and objectively with Chronotest software and the Trail Making Test; both manic and depressed subjects were slow in the Trail Making Test, but the subjective experience of time was slowed in the depressed, sped up in the manic and unchanged in controls.

Age disorientation (chronic schizophrenia) is defined as misstating one's age by 5 or more years; approximately ==25%== of patients in chronic care facilities are age disoriented. Most understate their age; a further ==10%== report an incorrect subjective age within 5 years of their age at illness onset. These patients are generally older, with a longer current admission and younger at first admission; it is associated with early onset and poor prognosis.

sections.title: 3. Disorders of perception: distortions, imagery and illusions

blocks.text: Perception has two parts: receiving information from a sensory modality (bottom up) and instantaneous interpretation using cognitive faculties (top down). Normally any perceived object corresponds to the stimulus that elicited it. Perception occurs in visual, auditory, tactile, gustatory, olfactory, kinaesthetic or proprioceptive modalities, and distortions can occur in any of these.

In a perceptual distortion a stimulus is perceived as the corresponding object but inaccurately (changes in size, shape, intensity, colour). Perception is dulled in depression and hypoactive delirium; intense perceptions occur in mania, hyperactive delirium and drug-induced states (hallucinogens). Hyperacusis especially is seen in migraine and alcohol hangover.

blocks.title: Distortions of shape and size
rows: Changes in the shape of objects, especially with loss of symmetry

blocks.text: These distortions are usually organic: ictal (parietal) or ocular (accommodation errors; paralysed accommodation can cause micropsia), rarely in acute schizophrenia. Hallucinogens (mescalin) can also change the colour of perceived objects or make components of an object, e.g. body parts, appear detached in space.

Hyperaesthesia is keyed when the **INTENSITY** of a percept changes without sensory distortion (a vivid red carpet, cheers 'louder than thousands of pneumatic drills') - the explanation contrasts it with macropsia, dysmegalopsia and illusions, where the quality changes instead.

Pseudo-hallucinations are the odd one out among sensory distortions - hyperacusis, hyperaesthesia, macropsia and dysmegalopsia are all changes in the perceived intensity or quality of a real external stimulus.

blocks.text: Imagery is not a perception: no stimulus is involved and no object perceived; it is essentially a fantasy. Imagery refers to images produced voluntarily with complete insight that they are mental, not external; they lack the objective quality of hallucinations and normal sense perceptions.

Eidetic imagery is a special memory ability in which visual images are drawn from memory accurately at will and described as if being perceived currently. It is noted in children (2-==15%== of school goers) and may be part of religious experiences; no pathological association is noted consistently.

Illusions may be difficult to differentiate from hallucinations if the source of the stimulus is hard to trace (e.g. 'Did I see the devil on the wall or from the wallpaper pattern?'), but they are qualitatively different and patiently eliciting the description helps. There are three major types.

blocks.title: Three types of illusion
rows: Prevailing emotional state leads to misperceptions
Disappears on focussing the object with extra concentration
Formed objects from ambiguous stimuli, coloured by prevailing emotion; not entirely due to inattention or affective change
On paying extra effort, the object intensifies - does not disappear
Stimulus that does not form a complete object might be perceived to be complete
Disappearance on concentration is the rule

blocks.text: 'Illusions occur when the perception threshold is increased' is the **FALSE** statement to spot - illusions can be brought on by sensory deprivation, visual illusions are influenced by prevailing emotional tone, and both affect and complete illusions resolve on closer attention.

bullets.text: Perception = bottom-up reception + top-down interpretation; errors: distortion (stimulus, object, quality altered), illusion (stimulus, different object), hallucination (no stimulus), negative hallucination (stimulus, no object).
Dulled perception: depression, hypoactive delirium; intense perception: mania, hyperactive delirium, hallucinogens; hyperacusis in migraine and alcohol hangover.
Dysmegalopsia = shape change/loss of symmetry; micropsia = shrinking; macropsia = enlarging; usually organic (ictal parietal, ocular).
Imagery: voluntary, with insight, no stimulus - a fantasy, not a perception; eidetic imagery: accurate visual recall at will, children 2-15%, religious experiences.
Three illusions: affect (emotion; disappears on concentration), pareidolic (ambiguous stimulus, playful; intensifies on effort), completion (inattention; disappears on concentration).
Pareidolia: common in febrile delirium in children and hallucinogen use; some voluntary control; not characteristic of psychosis.

sections.title: 4. Disorders of perception: pseudohallucinations and the qualities of hallucinations

blocks.text: Although the distinction between pseudohallucination and hallucination is not always clinically relevant, presentation with consistent pseudohallucinations and no other psychotic features should make one question the veracity of the psychopathology.

blocks.title: Two definitions of pseudohallucination
rows: Involuntary hallucination-like experiences occurring in inner subjective space, with a vivid outline, that are absolutely different from normal sense perceptions and hallucinations
Hallucinations that are recognised to be unreal and self-originating

blocks.text: European psychopathologists use the former definition more often. Pseudohallucinations are not pathognomonic of anything and are not always pathological.

Pseudohallucinations are intermediate between fantasy (imagery) and hallucinations. Like fantasy they are in subjective space, lack the quality of concrete reality, have the quality of an idea so are not sought in other modalities simultaneously (no searching, no reaching out) and are appreciated to be observer-dependent and self-originating. Like a hallucination they have a clear outline, are vivid, retained for a good length of time, cannot be dismissed at will and are behaviourally and emotionally relevant (acted upon or felt for).

'Images are incomplete with ill-defined outlines' is the false statement about pseudohallucinations - the explanation says they resemble true hallucinations in most respects except retained insight and occurrence in inner subjective (not outer objective) space.
The hallucinatory experiences of bereavement and in Ganser's state are pseudohallucinations.

blocks.title: True hallucination vs pseudohallucination
rows: Not sought in other modalities usually
Often in personality disorders, following trauma, dissociative experiences

blocks.title: Five qualities that distinguish hallucinations from other mental phenomena
rows: They take place at the same time as other sensory perceptions
The voice is heard even when music is playing or someone is talking; different from dreams where no real component exists alongside the false perception
They take place in the same space as other perceptions
An angel seen standing at the corner of my room; different from fantasy or imagery in subjective space
They are experienced as sensations, not as thoughts
The percept has all qualities of an object
Believed to be experienceable in other modalities, so hallucinators search for the man behind the voice or reach out to touch visual percepts
Appearance cannot be controlled; they exist even when not perceived by the hallucinator; may lack publicness - not everyone could hear and see them

bullets.text: Pseudohallucination definitions: Kandinsky/Jaspers/Sims (inner subjective space, vivid outline, involuntary - used more in Europe) vs Hare (recognised as unreal and self-originating).
Not pathognomonic of anything, not always pathological; bereavement and Ganser's state hallucinations are pseudohallucinations.
Intermediate between fantasy and hallucination: subjective space, not sought in other modalities, observer-dependent - yet vivid, clear outline, cannot be dismissed at will, emotionally relevant.

True hallucination: objective space, no insight, sought in other modalities, psychosis; pseudo: subjective space, insight often, not sought in other modalities, personality disorders/trauma/dissociation.
Hallucination qualities: simultaneous with other perceptions, in same space, experienced as sensations not thoughts, object-like (hallucinators search for the voice), involuntary and independent.
Consistent pseudohallucinations with no other psychotic features should make one question the psychopathology.

sections.title: 5. Disorders of perception: auditory and visual hallucinations

blocks.text: Elementary, unstructured auditory hallucinations are seen in acute organic states. Formed auditions such as voices (as in thought echo) cannot be elementary.
Musical hallucinations are similar to Charles Bonnet syndrome in the visual domain: they can occur in those with deafness and also in organic conditions.

Phonemes are any auditory hallucinations occurring as human voices. Schizophrenic phonemes are usually multiple, may or may not be recognisable, usually male with a different accent, speaking in one's mother tongue, and usually episodic - almost never continuous.

Verbal transformation effect: when the same word is repeated continuously, normal subjects hear phonetically linked but different words, whereas hallucinating schizophrenia subjects hear different words with no phonetic connection to the original word.

Patients can be distracted away from their voices, but the attention paid to the external stimulus matters more than the degree of external stimulus used. Alcoholic hallucinosis initially starts as fragmented voices, later organised into clear voices.

Causes of visual hallucinations: occipital lobe tumours, postconcussional states, epileptic twilight state, hepatic failure (any toxic delirium) and dementia. ==30%== of old age psychiatric referrals have visual hallucinations. Solvent sniffing and hallucinogens can cause elementary visual hallucinations such as light flashes. Simultaneous visual-verbal hallucinations (a green man speaking to me) are seen in temporal lobe epilepsy.
Visual hallucinations are very uncommon in schizophrenia (though Andreasen quotes ==30%== in a series observed with acute schizophrenia).

A hospitalised elderly patient seeing small angels: 'presence of intact consciousness suggests a functional disorder rather than an organic one' is the **LEAST** true option - the explanation says visual hallucinations are characteristic of organic states (voices of schizophrenia), and anticholinergic toxicity and delirium tremens are both valid causes.

blocks.text: 'Black patch' psychosis was frequently reported after simultaneous bilateral cataract surgery in the early era, attributed to sensory deprivation (leading to operating on one eye at a time); it was subsequently recognised as a relatively uncommon postoperative delirium, partly due to anticholinergic eye drops.

Charles Bonnet syndrome: elderly patients with normal consciousness and no brain pathology, with reduced visual acuity due to ocular problems, experience vivid, distinct, usually well-coloured formed hallucinations (mostly humans, at times animals and cartoons). The objects usually show movement and can be voluntarily controlled (disappear on closing the eyes); insight is usually preserved though they may evoke fear or joy. About a third are elementary; the hallucinations are usually located in external space.

Complex visual hallucinations in a partially sighted elderly woman with no psychotic features are keyed to 'she may retain insight' (Charles Bonnet) - the explanation says clear consciousness, no psychopathology, central **OR** peripheral visual reduction, and images that may be static or in motion, which is why the 'altered consciousness' and 'objects usually static' options are wrong.

sections.title: 6. Disorders of perception: somatic, olfactory, hypnagogic, functional and reflex hallucinations; synaesthesia

blocks.title: Somatic hallucinations
rows: Tactile (haptic - touch), hygric (fluid - wetness) and thermic (heat or cold)
Usually pain-like sensations from deep viscera like the liver; sometimes termed coenesthetic hallucinations and suggest schizophrenia
Joint or muscle sense, often linked to bizarre somatic delusions; also seen in benzodiazepine withdrawal and alcohol intoxication
A special haptic type (formic acid, from ant): unpleasant sensation of little animals or insects crawling under the skin; seen in delirium tremens and cocaine intoxication

blocks.text: Tactile hallucinations can be seen in parietal seizures. Superficial somatic hallucinations are almost never noted in temporal lobe epilepsy, though the visceral sense of 'raising epigastrium' is seen.

The common experience of the phantom limb is a body image disturbance, not a hallucination: though in external space it does not satisfy the other qualities of hallucination and patients are usually aware of its unreality; it has a neurological basis.

Recurrent sensations from an amputated limb are keyed to body image disturbance, **NOT** hallucination - the explanation says the phantom limb is produced by peripheral and central disorders, whereas a hallucination in the strict sense must occur in the absence of a stimulus.

blocks.text: Somatic hallucinations may or may not be accompanied by passivity delusions; without passivity delusions they cannot be classed as a first rank symptom.

blocks.title: Olfactory, gustatory and extracampine hallucinations
rows: Can occur in the aura of temporal lobe epilepsy (usually burning or urine smell); in depression can be an adjunct to nihilism
E.g. the bitter taste of poison can give rise to delusions of persecution in schizophrenia; also seen in temporal lobe epilepsy

Occur outside the normal field of perception (images seen behind your back, under your sternum, voices from Inverness); occur in schizophrenia, epilepsy and in hypnagogic hallucinations of healthy people - so not diagnostically important

blocks.text: Illusions and hallucinations are not necessarily pathological. Hypnagogic hallucinations (when going to sleep - the notes' memory aid is 'go for gogic'; usually auditory, but can be visual or tactile; also seen in narcolepsy-cataplexy; first noted by Aristotle) and hypnopompic hallucinations (when waking up) can occur in normal individuals. Hallucinations also occur in glue sniffing, post-infective depression, children with fevers and phobic anxiety; sensory deprivation in healthy people can produce them. They are not more frequent in schizophrenia than in other conditions.

A voice heard on drifting to sleep 'can occur in the absence of a diagnosable mental illness' - the explanation says hypnagogic hallucinations are most commonly visual or auditory, sometimes seen in narcolepsy or affective illness, but not indicative of ill health and frequently reported by healthy people; 'only auditory', 'beta rhythm' and 'sign of nocturnal epilepsy' are wrong.

blocks.text: Functional hallucinations: an external stimulus provokes a hallucination, both in the same modality but individually perceived (e.g. voices heard whenever the noise of water running through the tap is heard). They are not illusions, as the stimulus is perceived appropriately (noise of water) but there is in addition another perception (voices) without any appropriate object.

Voices heard whenever running tap water is heard are a **FUNCTIONAL** hallucination - the explanation says both the stimulus and the hallucination are experienced, in the same modality, and the hallucination requires the real sensation; reflex, reverse and extracampine hallucination are the look-alike options.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/5) Descriptive Psychopathology Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Reflex hallucinations: hallucinations in one modality provoked reflexively by a stimulus in another modality (e.g. seeing an angel whenever listening to music). Like functional hallucinations there is a normally perceived stimulus followed by a hallucinatory perception; the difference is that the modality of stimulus and perception is the same in functional and different in reflex hallucinations.

blocks.caption: Two-column comparison box. Synesthesia: 1 'Music is seen as colours'; 2 often only one perception ('music gets seen'), sometimes both stimulus and object are perceived; 3 object perceived corresponds to stimulus though in different modality; 4 at same time (syn - simultaneous); 5 percepts are often simple and unformed e.g. colours. Reflex hallucination: 1 'On hearing running tap water, an angel is seen'; 2 both stimulus and objects are perceived separately; 3 perceptions are in different modality but object does not correspond to image; 4 one after another - not simultaneous; 5 percepts are often fully formed, complex or bizzare e.g. angel's face.

blocks.title: Reflex hallucination vs synaesthesia
rows: Stimulus perceived, then a hallucinated percept (the patient claims to see Jesus or an angel)
The music itself is seen - stimulus and object of perception remain the same, in a different modality
Formed voices, vivid images like angels
Stimulus-perception sequence usually completed before the hallucination ('I heard the music and then came the angel')
Both stimulus and hallucinated object perceived separately
Often only one perception ('the music gets seen'); sometimes both stimulus and object are perceived
Perceived object does not correspond to the stimulus (running tap water does not correspond with an angel)
Perceived object corresponds to the stimulus, though in a different modality

blocks.text: Synaesthesia: first reported by Francis Galton (1880). The perception of a stimulus of one modality in a different modality (e.g. tasting the music, hearing colours, smelling voices). It is not a hallucination as the perceived object has an appropriate stimulus, and the original stimulus is usually perceived in the appropriate modality too (syn = joint, simultaneous). Common in females (4:1 to 6:1), runs in families, colour-number synaesthesia the most common form. Thought to be due to extensive cross wiring between multimodal association regions, probably from failed selective pruning.

Evidence for a neural basis of synaesthesia: consistency of associations over time (Baron-Cohen: ==92%== of colour-sound associations after 1 year in 13 synaesthetes vs ==37%== after 1 week in controls); it can be acquired in neurological illness (multiple sclerosis, temporal arteritis, tumours of the sella region); it can be induced by drugs such as mescaline; and cerebral blood flow differs between synaesthetes and non-synaesthetes.

sections.title: 7. Delusions: definition, continuum, persistence and dimensions

blocks.text: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition defines a delusion as 'A false belief ... that is firmly sustained despite what almost everyone else believes and despite what constitutes incontrovertible and obvious proof or evidence to the contrary'. This definition, though useful, conceals the multidimensionality of delusional experience.

Some authors suggest delusions and hallucinations are commonplace in healthy populations (prevalence up to approximately ==25%== depending on definitional criteria), so that psychosis exists in a continuum model; this claim is yet to be validated and established (Lincoln, 2007).

Using self-report measures only, Lincoln (2007) found that high distress associated with beliefs appears a relevant characteristic of delusions in schizophrenia compared with 'delusion-like beliefs in common population'; the presence of hallucinatory experiences accompanying delusions did not differ between the two.

Persistence: in a follow-up of nearly 1100 acutely hospitalised psychiatric patients re-interviewed at 10-week intervals for 1 year, most delusions showed a high degree of plasticity and in nearly one-third delusions completely subsided (Applebaum et al. 2004).

Delusional ideation is more likely to persist in never married, older patients, those with schizophrenia, with delusions of thought broadcasting, with a higher degree of preoccupation and behavioural relevance, and with more than one primary delusion. Even when delusional experience persists, the same delusion is not necessarily maintained; considerable change in content was noted.

The extent to which the belief extends to various spheres of life

Most bizarre delusions are Schneiderian (first rank symptoms type)
The extent to which the patient is preoccupied and distressed
The extent to which the belief drives behaviour

The extent to which the patient questions the veracity of the belief or seeks to strengthen it; often patients do not need external proof and will continue to hold the belief despite contrary evidence

sections.title: 8. Delusions: primary and secondary delusions

blocks.text: Primary delusions are defined in two ways: (1) Jaspers' concept - true, un-understandable beliefs that arrive fully formed and cannot be reduced further to any other mental experience (recently challenged); (2) the first psychopathology to occur in the course of symptoms (temporal sequence). Often both are true: they are irreducible and precede other mental phenomena.

blocks.title: The four types of primary delusion
rows: Ideas that occur de novo, 'out of the blue', taking form in an instant without identifiable preceding events, like a bolt from the blue; can be an elaborate delusional system on arrival. Wernicke formulated the concept; autochthonous = 'out of soil', 'aboriginal'

A normally perceived object is given a new meaning, usually self-reference; the conclusion is entirely unwarranted while the perception is normal. A two-staged process (normal perception, then delusional significance) whose steps need not be simultaneous and might be separated for years. The only delusion included in Schneider's first-rank symptoms

Sense of perplexity and uncertainty during a prodrome of psychosis, usually ending in an autochthonous delusion that makes sense of the perplexity; can precede other primary delusions. The only psychiatric phenomenon that can directly precede and be causally related to a primary autochthonous delusion. A specific affective experience, not thought content

Retrospective delusion (something that never happened reported as recollected, e.g. 'I had a hysterectomy at age 3 and since then I became a man') or a normal memory delusionally elaborated ('My dad bought me a camera when I was seven, now I understand it is because he was homosexual')

blocks.text: Delusional misidentification is the odd one out among the primary delusions - the four types are delusional mood (atmosphere), delusional perception, delusional memory and autochthonous delusion; the same stem is repeated in a mock exam.

blocks.text: 'Delusional mood is a first rank symptom of schizophrenia' is the **FALSE** statement - the explanation says delusional mood (delusional atmosphere) is a primary delusion but **NOT** a first-rank symptom; it is profoundly apprehensive, perplexed and often followed by a fully formed delusion.

blocks.text: Delusional perception can mimic delusional memory when the first-stage normal perception is a 'recollected' normal perception from memory, but it remains a two-stage process (e.g. 'I saw an envelope yesterday [normal perception recollected from memory], I realised my stomach is upturned').

Primary delusions carry no prognostic significance in schizophrenia though they have diagnostic relevance. They can occur in epileptic psychoses, but are not generally associated with epilepsy when they occur in psychotic disorders. They occur more in acute stages of schizophrenia and are not seen in chronic schizophrenia, where they are mixed with secondary delusions, hallucinations, formal thought disorder etc. Delusions that follow a primary delusion or other mental phenomena (hallucinations, affective disturbances) are secondary delusions.

sections.title: 9. Delusions: paranoid, monothematic and hypochondriacal content

blocks.text: The term paranoid is very much misused in psychiatric practice. Paranoia stands for 'besides mind'. In the strict sense, 'paranoid' can be used only for self-referential delusions, irrespective of content: e.g. grandiose ('God is sending a messiah to help me'), persecutory ('mafia is after me'), referential ('those kids are talking about me, cameras are fixed to watch me') and hypochondriacal or nihilistic ('my body is rotting away') are all paranoid delusions.
Monothematic delusions can occur as single delusions in various disorders, in their commonest form in major psychotic illnesses like schizophrenia or affective psychosis.

blocks.title: Monothematic delusions and example content
rows: "That's not my wife; it is an impostor who looks just like her."
"I am constantly being followed by people I know, but I can't recognize them because they are always in disguise."
"The person I see when I look in the mirror isn't me; it is some stranger who looks like me."
"Person X is secretly in love with me" (Person X being some important or famous person who has never encouraged this idea)

blocks.text: Morbid jealousy can occur in various forms - delusion, overvalued idea, in depression and in anxiety states; it is not a misidentification syndrome. First described by Ey. It is common in alcoholics, has a potential for violence (especially against the rival rather than the partner) and can occur among cohabiters and homosexual couples too.

De Clerambault's syndrome is a type of delusion of love in which a woman believes that an older man of higher social status is in love with her. It is not related to delusional misidentification. It is also called Old Maid's insanity, where persecutory beliefs coexist.

Cotard's syndrome is severe depression with nihilistic and hypochondriacal delusions tinged with grandiosity and a negative attitude; it is not related to delusional misidentification. Seen in schizophrenia, though more commonly in depressive psychosis; generally in the elderly, with a tinge of grandiosity amidst nihilism (not grandiose delusions). Also reported in organic lesions and migraine.

Couvade syndrome is the mismatched pairing - it is **NOT** a delusion of pregnancy in postpartum mothers but a conversion symptom in partners of expectant mothers; Othello-jealousy, De Clerambault-love, Cotard-nihilistic and Ekbom-infestation are the correct pairings.

blocks.text: Hypochondriacal delusions are typically seen in psychotic depression, especially in the elderly, as part of Cotard's syndrome. Munro's monosymptomatic hypochondriacal psychosis consists of (1) delusions of body odour and halitosis (olfactory delusions) - some of these may have olfactory reference syndrome (no olfactory experiences, only a fixed belief about body odour with anxiety reaction; paranoid personality disorder is often associated).

(2) Delusional infestation (Ekbom's syndrome): a delusion of parasitic, macroscopic infestation with the classical matchbox sign - an old lady comes to clinic with a match box of skin scrapings as evidence for the parasite causing her itching. It can predate the onset of dementia and may or may not be associated with a somatic hallucination.
(3) Dysmorphic delusions (misshaped nose, etc.) are listed as the third component of monosymptomatic hypochondriacal psychosis.

sections.title: 10. Delusions: misidentification syndromes

blocks.text: The various misidentification syndromes (Ellis, 2005) are described below.

blocks.title: Delusional misidentification syndromes
rows: A person usually close to the patient has been replaced by an exact double (sometimes called the illusion of doubles, though it is a delusion). First reported by Kahlbaum (1866), described more extensively by Capgras and colleagues (1923, 1924). Classified as a dangerous delusion, may be associated with violence; etiologically heterogeneous (at least 15 different causes); mostly due to organic brain damage (>==50%==, Lishman) apart from schizophrenia or isolated delusional disorder

False identification of familiar persons in strangers; a familiar person is thought to be taking various disguises. First reported by Courbon and Fail (1927). No belief in actual physical change - the patient believes persecutors can invade the body of others. Rare compared to Capgras. Original case (Courbon and Fail): a 27-year-old woman, a domestic servant with a passion for the theatre, who developed the delusion that the actresses Robin and Sarah Bernhardt were persecuting her in the guise of others; the term Fregoli delusion refers to the celebrated Italian mimic Leopoldo Fregoli
The patient believes another person has been physically transformed into his own self and is convinced exact doubles of him- or herself exist

A becomes C, C becomes B etc.: people keep transforming their physical and psychological identities (Courbon and Tusques 1932: Sylvie G, 49 years). No further reports for 46 years, then five cases, three of them by Young et al. (1990)

Very rare, re-described by Ellis (Krauss, 1852): a face appears to transform within seconds into a grotesque mask ('monster', 'vampire', 'werewolf'). Most likely reported by schizophrenic children, also in adults (e.g. Schreber saw two men 'as devils with particularly red faces')

blocks.text: Cotard syndrome is the odd one out among delusional misidentification syndromes - Fregoli, Capgras, subjective doubles and reduplicative paramnesia were the other options; the explanation lists Capgras, Fregoli, intermetamorphosis, subjective doubles, autoscopic, reverse subjective double and reverse Fregoli as the types.

sections.title: 11. Delusions: ideas of reference, overvalued ideas, folie a deux and how delusions form

blocks.text: Ideas of reference are seen in paranoid personality disorder, where the individual is unduly self-conscious and feels that people take notice of him or observe things about him he would rather not be seen. They can precede full-blown schizophrenia, where they are called sensitive ideas of reference ('sensitiver Beziehungswahn'). They are not characteristic of mania.

Overvalued ideas (Wernicke) are solitary abnormal beliefs that are neither delusional nor obsessional, but dominate a person's life and actions. They have a poor prognosis. Common conditions presenting with overvalued ideas: paranoid or anankastic personality disorder, body dysmorphophobia, anorexia nervosa, morbid jealousy and transsexualism.

Folie a deux is a shared delusion in which a psychotic person transfers his delusions to one or more people close to him. The non-psychotic victim usually exhibits dependent traits on the primary patient. Separation of the pair can result in remission.

Doppelganger (the double phenomenon) is the awareness of oneself as both outside and inside oneself. It is a cognitive and ideational disturbance, as opposed to autoscopy, which is a perceptual disturbance. It can occur in the absence of mental illness and is not a delusional misidentification syndrome (the latter is a pathology of familiarity).

blocks.title: How are delusions formed? (models in the notes)
rows: People with persecutory delusions preferentially attend to threat-related stimuli and preferentially recall threatening episodes (Blackwood, American Journal of Psychiatry 2001)

Exaggerated self-serving attribution bias in psychosis: positive events attributed to internal causes (stable, global - grandiose), negative events to external causes (stable, global - persecutory). The bias shapes delusional content rather than form; paranoid patients attribute negative self-referent events to active malevolence of the other person (external personal) rather than circumstances or chance (external situational), possibly preserving self-esteem

In the beads task deluded patients decide with far fewer beads than controls and are overconfident; later studies showed that given as many beads as controls they reach similar correct conclusions, so the defect is deficient data-gathering (less information before decision)
Persecutory delusions reflect false beliefs about the intentions and behaviour of others that could arise from theory of mind deficits

sections.title: 12. First Rank Symptoms

blocks.text: Kurt Schneider, a German psychiatrist and pupil of Karl Jaspers, pointed out certain symptoms as characteristic of schizophrenia and therefore of 'first-rank' status in the hierarchy of potentially diagnostic symptoms.

In International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision and Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 3rd-4th editions the presence of one first rank symptom is symptomatically sufficient for the diagnosis of schizophrenia, but first rank symptoms are not essential to the diagnosis. First rank symptoms may also be encountered in non-schizophrenic conditions, so they are not specific or diagnostic for schizophrenia (Palaniyappan, 2007).

Schneider proposed an empirical cluster of symptoms, one or more of which, in the absence of evidence of organic processes, could be used as positive evidence for schizophrenia. He did not claim they were comprehensive, but they are clearly identifiable, frequently occurring and more frequent in schizophrenia than any other disorder.

First rank symptoms emphasise the form of the experience rather than its content (that voices echo one's thoughts matters more than what they actually say). Disturbance of self-image (ego-boundary) is the predominant underlying feature of all first rank symptoms.

Nordgaard et al. (2008): first rank symptoms occur in ==22%== to ==29%== of patients with affective disorders; their prevalence in schizophrenia ranges between ==25%== and ==88%==, equally high in western and developing countries and across ethnic groups. In some studies delusional perception is the most frequent first rank symptoms, in others the least frequent; no single type dominates.

The question keys 'first rank symptoms may present in 10-==25%== of manic patients' (never, very rarely and all cases are the wrong options), whereas the notes give 22-==29%== for affective disorders - the shared point is that first rank symptoms are not pathognomonic and also occur in bipolar mania, temporal lobe epilepsy and organic psychotic states.

Assessment of the diagnostic weight of individual first rank symptoms is absent, except Mellor and colleagues, who suggest that 'voices discussing' should be given less diagnostic weight. The majority of reports conclude that first rank symptoms do not affect outcome: no study finds outcome related to the number of first rank symptoms; first rank symptoms are not of any prognostic importance, and do not specify subgroups with differential treatment response or heritability.
'First rank symptoms carry prognostic significance' is the **FALSE** statement - they are neither pathognomonic nor specific to schizophrenia and are also seen in organic and affective psychoses.

Voices **COMMANDING** the patient are **NOT** first rank (command/teleological hallucinations) - voices commenting, discussing among themselves and echoing the patient's thoughts are.

blocks.title: Disorders of phonation and articulation
rows: Inability to vocalise: a disturbance of sound production (phonation) rather than sound manipulation (articulation). Whispering occurs; due to paralysed vocal cords or hysteria
Disorder of articulation; may be due to lesions in the brain stem (bulbar), cortex (pseudobulbar), cerebellum or extrapyramidal system; can also be drug induced in schizophrenia
Normal flow of speech interrupted by pauses or repetition of fragments or parts of words; tics often accompany; boys more often than girls; usually reduced in adulthood

Difficulty uttering speech sounds at the beginning of words; utterances repetitive, prolonged, pauses common. Primary stuttering is seen in children; new onset in adults may relate to stroke or extrapyramidal symptoms

Accelerated talking seen in manic states
Increased quantity of speech, generally without pressure of speech or formal thought disturbance; seen especially in early manic states

Poverty of speech and decrease in spontaneous talking; occurs in depression and schizophrenia. Differentiate from poverty of content of speech (amount adequate but little information), often related to schizophrenic formal thought disorder
Complete lack of speech. Severe depression with psychomotor retardation may be associated with mutism, though rare in the absence of catatonia; almost always present in a catatonic stupor

Stammering: pauses and repeated word fragments, tics, boys > girls; stuttering: difficulty with initial speech sounds; adult onset may follow stroke or extrapyramidal disease.
Bradyphasia: slow speech in depression; tachyphasia: fast speech in mania; logorrhoea: more speech, early mania; alogia: poverty of speech in depression and schizophrenia.

Mutism: complete lack of speech; severe depression with retardation may cause it, rarely without catatonia; almost always in catatonic stupor; elective mutism in children who refuse to speak to certain people.

Hysterical mutism is rare (aphonia is the commonest hysterical speech disorder); akinetic mutism: upper midbrain/posterior diencephalon lesions, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease; aware but cannot move or respond.

sections.title: 14. Disturbed language processing: aphasias, reading and writing disorders

blocks.text: Sound received by the ears is transmitted to Wernicke's area and the auditory association cortex, which process the language component. The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke's area to Broca's area, the higher motor area of language production. Signals from Broca's area are relayed to the motor area to coordinate delivery of language via the tongue, lips and vocal cords.

blocks.caption: Diagram: Ears arrow to Wernicke's area (A); arrow B (arcuate fasciculus, conduction aphasia) from Wernicke's area to Broca's area (C); Broca's area arrow to Peripheral speech areas (tongue, lips); Wernicke's area arrow D to Auditory association cortex; Language association cortex arrow E to Broca's area. Key box: A Sensory aphasia (Wernicke's); B Arcuate fasciculus lesion - conduction aphasia; C Broca's aphasia; D Transcortical sensory aphasia; E Transcortical motor aphasia. Fluency: E to C is required; Comprehension: A to D is required; Repetition: A to B to C is required.

blocks.title: Components of language production
rows: Production of meaningful words and sentences; depends on intact Broca's area and its forward connections
Understanding words and sentences spoken by others; depends on intact Wernicke's area and its connection with association cortex and sensory input
Repeating what others say; requires no high-level processing; can take place if Broca's, Wernicke's and the arcuate fasciculus are intact; needs no relay of higher association area to either
Ability to use nouns, especially names of objects; naming defects (anomia) accompany any aphasia in various degrees

blocks.title: Lesion sites in the language pathway
rows: Connection from Wernicke's area to the auditory association cortex
Connection from the language association cortex to Broca's area

blocks.text: Pathways required: fluency needs E to C (language association cortex to Broca's area); comprehension needs A to D (Wernicke's area to auditory association cortex); repetition needs A to B to C (Wernicke's area, arcuate fasciculus, Broca's area).
Aphasia is a higher-level 'language' problem - not a sound production or manipulation error but a problem of language reception, production and processing. It is almost always organic.

blocks.title: Types of aphasia (adapted from Harrison's Textbook of Internal Medicine, 15th ed.)

blocks.text: In Broca's aphasia speech is nonfluent, often laboured with interruptions and pauses. Function words (prepositions, conjunctions) are most affected, though a good degree of meaning-appropriate nouns and verbs are still produced. Abnormal word order and a characteristic agrammatism are noted; speech is telegraphic. The notes quote Harrison's textbook example: "I see...the dotor, dotor sent me...Bosson. Go to hospital. Dotor...kept me beside. Two, tee days, doctor send me home".

In Wernicke's aphasia comprehension is impaired for both spoken and written language. Output is fluent but highly paraphasic, sometimes with strings of neologisms and circumlocutions, hence 'jargon aphasia'. The speech contains large numbers of function words but few substantive nouns or verbs referring to specific actions: voluminous but uninformative.
As aphasia is a disturbance of language production, reading and writing difficulties accompany all aphasias. In addition, some isolated reading/writing disorders have been described.

blocks.title: Isolated disorders of reading and writing
rows: Patient speaks normally, comprehends speech, writes spontaneously and to dictation, but reading comprehension is impaired
Isolated inability to write with other language faculties preserved; sometimes a component of Gerstmann's syndrome (parietal deficits)

Patient can speak, read and write fluently but comprehension is impaired only for spoken language; bilateral (or left-sided with disrupted connections to the non-dominant circuit) damage to the superior temporal pole is suspected
Spoken language cannot be produced clearly, but the patient comprehends language well and can read and write

sections.title: 15. Disorders of thought: normal thinking and the classification of formal thought disorder

blocks.title: Three types of normal thinking
rows: No goal direction, unrealistic, daydreaming type; predominant in cluster A personality, dissociation and pseudologia fantastica
Fantasy elements admixed with memory, involving abstract concepts, but goal-directed and not crossing boundaries of possibility and realism; determining tendency preserved, e.g. lateral thinking
Based on factual reality and uses logic

blocks.text: Psychopathology of thought includes (1) disorders of thought content (e.g. delusions), (2) thought form (e.g. tangentiality), (3) thought stream (e.g. pressure of speech) and (4) thought control (e.g. obsessions).

blocks.title: Elements of thought (supermarket analogy)
rows: Bags, boxes, sold loose as single fruit? - 'the package'
In what manner is the thought present?
Packed as a dozen, a score, just four, half a dozen; fast, slow - 'the amount'
How is it being thought about?
Poverty of thought, pressure of speech and crowding of thoughts
Mango is a produce of South Africa; tomatoes are from Spain - 'the origin'
To some extent obsessions, passivity and first rank thought disturbances

blocks.text: Thought content can be deciphered from behaviour, but thought form and stream, unless extremely deranged, cannot be studied without being expressed as speech. Formal thought disorder refers to disturbances in form and not content; it is wrong to say 'someone is deluded so he has a formal thought disorder'.
The term formal thought disorder increasingly includes both form and stream errors (not content errors), and scales that measure thought disorder no longer differentiate stream from form.

Various authors have used various terms for formal thought disorder, so there is significant overlap and the terms are not mutually exclusive. Paralogia refers to positive formal thought disorder (presence of an abnormal element in thought processes, e.g. tangentiality); alogia is sometimes used for negative formal thought disorder (absence of a normal element, e.g. poverty of speech content). Kraepelin used akataphasia; Bleuler's 'loosening of associations' is often considered to indicate formal thought disorder.

blocks.title: Cameron's four formal thought disorders
rows: Imprecise approximate expressions used as substitute words (e.g. 'paperskate' for a pen)

Lack of genuine causal links in speech (e.g. 'I got up at eight this morning as well as few birds of different colours on the painting, shrinking all the time to drop few coins. On the floor. All the time.')

Ideas only remotely related to the concept under consideration are incorporated; conceptual boundaries are lost. Used to explain thought disorder in schizophrenia and different from the mechanism in flight of ideas; tested with sorting tests; occurs in nearly ==50%== of schizophrenia patients, especially when acutely ill
Irrelevant thoughts penetrate the ongoing stream of thoughts

blocks.text: The mock keys 'Cameron described **DERAILMENT**' (the explanation says his analysis of 25 unmistakably schizophrenic patients led to the concept of asyndetic thinking, including derailment, loss of the central determining idea and loose associations) - whereas the notes tabulate Cameron's four as metonymy, asyndesis, overinclusion and interpenetration; know both framings.

blocks.title: Carl (not Kurt) Schneider's five elements of formal thought disorder
rows: One thought - often inappropriate - fills the gap between other appropriate, more consistent thoughts
A chunk of thought goes missing from the stream of conversation, patient unaware - best analysed when written
Various thoughts fuse together, leading to loss of goal direction
Disordered intermixture of constituent parts of one complex thought
The normally flowing track of thoughts suddenly changes; the determining tendency is preserved but misdirected

sections.title: 16. Disorders of thought: features of formal thought disorder, flight of ideas, circumstantiality, tangentiality and concrete thinking

blocks.title: Features of formal thought disorder
rows: Making up a totally new word not in the dictionary, or using a known word with a completely different meaning (e.g. 'Inkur' for pen (new); 'roast' for pen (different))

Newly synthesised or known words used in an idiosyncratic way repeatedly, often with many meanings in different contexts, sometimes dominating discourse (e.g. 'riposte', used in the notes' passage in turn for what appears to be a dog, a friend, energy and food - each marked '?' in the notes)

A negative formal thought disorder: sudden arrest in the flow of thoughts; sometimes resembles an absence seizure though there is no amnesia for the idea discussed and no typical motor accompaniments; patients can elaborate it with a delusional content of thought withdrawal

Pompous, formal speech, often in an inappropriate context; impaired lexical retrieval may underlie it in schizophrenia (e.g. 'Pliant rectitude is a trait more appropriate for successful living than hot-headedness...' - McKenna 1994)

blocks.text: Flight of ideas is characteristic of mania: thoughts follow each other so rapidly that there is no general direction; chance associations connect succeeding thoughts, arising from distractions in the environment (e.g. hearing a rustling newspaper while talking about breakfast and jumping to the Iraq war) or from elements of one's own or someone else's speech.

Speech linked from one sentence to the next by a word or idea ('soccer... shirts... clothes... dirty') is **FLIGHT** **OF** **IDEAS** - not loosening of association, paragrammatism, tangentiality or circumstantiality; the explanation says fragmented ideas are connected by distracting cues rather than the goal, common in mania.

blocks.title: Verbal associations cueing flight of ideas
rows: Thoughts associated by the initial syllabic structure of words rather than meaning (e.g. clover, cloud, clap, clan)
Words associated as one word has dual meaning (e.g. fast - 'to starve' or 'speed up')
Words associated by similar sounds (e.g. cat, rat, bat)

blocks.text: In schizophrenic formal thought disorder, clang occurs more often with first syllables, as opposed to clangs in poetry, humour and manic speech where they occur more at the end syllables.

Vorbeireden is talking past the point, giving approximate but not accurate answers to questions in an interview; a type of formal thought disorder different from flight of ideas. Though often described along with Ganser syndrome it is not exclusive to it; also seen in acute and hebephrenic schizophrenia. It is often used interchangeably with vorbeigehen ('going past the point'), which was originally defined as part of Ganser syndrome, where some criminals gave incorrect 'approximate answers' to simple questions that none the less suggested the correct answer was known (e.g. saying dogs have five legs).

blocks.title: Circumstantiality vs tangentiality
rows: Yes, eventually (a spiral that eventually touches its centre)
Never (a tangent scrapes through the edge and never reaches the centre)
Thinking proceeds slowly with many unnecessary details and digressions before returning to the point
The patient never reaches the point
Some patients with temporal lobe epilepsy, alcohol-induced persisting dementia, learning difficulty, obsessional personalities
Not stated separately in the notes

blocks.text: The notes add that circumstantiality is a formal thought disorder where figure-ground differentiation apparently fails, but not due to affective changes such as mania; it may be related to loosened associations, usually develops within the setting of a delusional mood in schizophrenia, and may be due to impairment of a central filtering process that normally inhibits irrelevant external sensations and internal thoughts.

'Circumstantiality - obsessive compulsive disorder' is the **INCORRECT** association - the explanation says circumstantial thinking can be seen in mania and obsessive-compulsive **PERSONALITY** disorder (not obsessive-compulsive disorder).

blocks.text: Concrete thinking is literalness of expression and understanding, with failed abstraction; it is recognisable clinically but difficult to measure by psychometry. Goldstein studied this loss of abstract thinking, which can be tested using proverbs and the similarities test. It is evident in speech-disordered (formal thought disorder) schizophrenia patients but not the non-**formal thought disorder** group (Allen 1984), and is also seen in fronto-temporal dementia.

sections.title: 17. Disorders of thought: testing linguistics, measuring and explaining schizophrenic speech disturbance

blocks.title: Testing the linguistics of schizophrenia
rows: Abnormal: despite the context, patients preferred the dominant meaning of a word (e.g. court = 'law-room', not tennis court, in a discussion about sports)
Parts of recorded speech are deleted to see if meaning can still be predicted; predictability was reduced in schizophrenia
Patients asked to predict the missing elements of someone else's speech; the schizophrenia group performed worse
Ratio between the number of different words and the total number of spoken words in a discourse; impoverished vocabulary = low type-token ratio in schizophrenia
Schizophrenia patients use fewer referential ties (pronouns without mentioning a subject first) and more lexical ties (connected words)
Patients make more errors than controls when constructing complex sentences from simple phrases

blocks.text: Formal thought disorder is measured with the Thought, Language and Communication scale (Andreasen) and the Thought and Language Index (Liddle); the latter uses projective stimuli from the Thematic Apperception Test to elicit thought disturbances.

Of the thought disorders classified by Andreasen, clanging and flight are more common in mania, while derailment (loosening), thought blocking and, to some extent, tangentiality and poverty of content of speech are seen often in schizophrenia; other items were largely non-specific. Formal thought disorder is suggestive but not pathognomonic of schizophrenia; it is also seen in organic syndromes such as epilepsy.

Of Andreasen's thought disorders, derailment (loosening), thought blocking and to some extent tangentiality and poverty of content of speech are more common in schizophrenia, whereas clanging and flight of ideas are more common in mania - the mock stem asks which is commoner in schizophrenia than mania.

blocks.title: Explanations of schizophrenic speech disturbance
rows: Formal thought disorder results from loss of deductive reasoning (illogical thinking): 'Kiwi cannot fly, Kiwi is a bird, so birds cannot fly' - inferences based on insufficient premises
Kelly's personal construct theory (repertory grids, Bannister)

Patient scores elements (relatives, friends) under constructs (qualities); in schizophrenia the predictability of an element's quality from prior constructs is affected - 'serial invalidation', more pronounced for people than objects, so thought disorder affects the interpersonal realm more; the scores can be used to draw a semantic space showing graphical connections between people and qualities in the patient's personal world
Associations between words and qualities are lost

Related words are cross-wired. Direct semantic priming (London - tube, Britain); indirect priming (London - tube - light) is usually minimal. In schizophrenia direct priming is proposed to be impaired and indirect priming activated more

Ability to understand that others have mental processes similar to self's; deficient in autistic children and can become acutely deficient (though developing normally) in schizophrenia during psychotic episodes; explains some pragmatic errors
The frontal lobe plays a role in language formation, so loss of executive function can cause poor planning, error monitoring and correction of speech production

Formal thought disorder scales: Thought, Language and Communication scale (Andreasen) and Thought and Language Index (Liddle; uses Thematic Apperception Test stimuli).
Clanging and flight more in mania; derailment, thought blocking, (tangentiality, poverty of content) more in schizophrenia; formal thought disorder suggestive, not pathognomonic; also in epilepsy.
Von Domarus: illogical reasoning from insufficient premises; Kelly: serial invalidation, worse for people than objects.
Semantic priming: direct priming impaired and indirect priming increased in schizophrenia (Mortimer: impaired semantic memory).
Theory-of-mind deficit (acute in psychosis) and dysexecutive problems proposed as bases for formal thought disorder.

sections.title: 18. Disorders of thought: stream and control (obsessions and compulsions)

blocks.text: Pressure of speech: excessive thoughts in mind accompanied by rapid, voluminous speech, often disjointed and non-pragmatic; seen in mania.

Crowding of thought occurs in schizophrenia: the patient describes thoughts as passively concentrated and compressed in the head; associations are experienced as excessive, too fast, inexplicable and outside the person's control. Experientially this is different from manic flight of ideas.

Retardation of thinking is seen in depression: the train of thought is slowed though goal-directed, with little initiative or planning, long latency of response and increased pause times when speech is initiated and during speech. In both this and pressure of speech the mood state of the patient dictates the flow of thoughts.

Perseveration is traditionally considered pathognomonic of organic brain disease: the thought process persists beyond the point at which it is relevant, presenting as the same answer or motor act repeated even though the stimulus has changed. It also occurs if there is clouded consciousness.

Giving the same answer ('cereals') to unrelated questions is **PERSEVERATION** - not stereotypy, mannerism, automatism or stuttering; the explanation says it continues a response after it ceases to be apposite and is associated with organic brain disease.

source.file: paper-a/High yields/CLASSIFICATION AND CLINICAL EXAMINATION/5) Descriptive Psychopathology Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Obsessions are unwanted, intrusive, repetitive, senseless thoughts experienced as troublesome and resisted; their appearance is appreciated to be beyond control but not due to external agency. Patients regard them as products of their own mind but against their values and needs - hence ego-alien. Intrusive thoughts occur before motor (compulsive) acts, but not every compulsion is preceded by an obsession or vice versa; primary obsessions often fade while compulsions dominate; some compulsions are mental (praying, counting).

A man who shouts 'Biance' whenever he sees a pretty woman is keyed to **COMPULSIVE** **ACT** (not obsessive impulse, obsessive image, mental compulsion or rumination) - the explanation says compulsive acts may not be preceded by an identifiable obsession in disorders such as autism, dementia and Tourette.

Obsessional slowness occurs either when obsessional thoughts are part of a depressive illness or in severe obsessive-compulsive disorder (primary obsessional slowness). Another pattern is obsession with symmetry or precision leading to a compulsion of slowness (hours to eat a meal or shave, doing things 'just right'); unlike other obsessive-compulsive disorder patients these patients do not resist their symptoms.

blocks.text: Fish classified motor symptoms into (a) abnormal spontaneous movements - tremors, tics, chorea, athetosis, stereotypy (noted in autistic spectrum disorders), hemiballismus etc. - and (b) abnormal induced movements: perseveration, automatic obedience, echo phenomenon and other catatonic signs.

blocks.text: Fink and Taylor have argued for catatonia as a separate taxonomy in psychiatric nosology. Catatonia is decreasing in frequency in its classical form, largely due to early diagnosis, treatment and deinstitutionalisation.

Catatonia is defined as rigidity during involuntary movements while volitional movement is carried out normally. In neurological spasticity the tone is increased irrespective of passive or active movement; a catatonic patient can use the affected limb with completely normal tone when needed (e.g. running out when there is a fire). Catatonia persists in sleep and can continue for weeks without improvement.

Catatonia is mostly seen in advanced primary mood or psychotic illnesses: among inpatients with a catatonic presentation, 25 to 50 percent are related to mood disorders and approximately 10 percent to schizophrenia. Catatonia results in both speech and motor disturbances.

blocks.title: Catatonic signs: compliance, opposition and blocking
rows: A schizophrenic patient brings the spoon to his mouth dozens of times but never completes the act: a series of tentative, opposing alternate movements that do not reach the goal (e.g. repeated protrusion and retraction of the tongue when asked to show it)

Exaggerated cooperation with the examiner's request or spontaneous continuation of the requested movement; the patient carries out instructions even when asked not to cooperate (Kraepelin pricked his patients' tongues with a pin each time they protruded them, yet they kept obeying)
The mildest form of automatic obedience: despite requests to resist manipulation, the patient yields to being placed in abnormal postures

The patient yields to the slightest pressure without much resistance, like an Anglepoise lamp, even if instructed to resist; may be a milder form of automatic obedience; also called 'magnet reaction' (follows the examiner around the room on light touch)
Wax-like, mouldable quality: limbs can be moved by the examiner to occupy postures that are then maintained even if uncomfortable and bizarre
Seen in catatonia, Latah (culture-bound) and Tourette's. Echopraxia = mimicking the examiner's movements; echolalia = mimicking the examiner's speech
Resistance to passive movement with strength proportional to the increase in muscle tone, which seems voluntarily controlled by the patient
Resisting or opposing all passive movements attempted by the examiner: an extreme form of opposition with apparently motiveless resistance to all interference; frustrating for carers
Like thought blocking but during motor acts: the patient suddenly stops a motor act for no reason, e.g. a requested movement is well begun then stops halfway

bullets.text: Fish: abnormal spontaneous movements (tremor, tics, chorea, athetosis, stereotypy, hemiballismus) vs abnormal induced movements (perseveration, automatic obedience, echo phenomenon, catatonic signs).
Catatonia = rigidity during involuntary movements with normal volitional movement (unlike spasticity); persists in sleep; 25-50% of catatonic inpatients mood disorder, ~10% schizophrenia.
Ambitendence: repeated tentative, opposing movements that never complete the act (spoon to mouth; tongue protruded then retracted).

Automatic obedience: complies even when asked not to (Kraepelin's tongue-pin); mitmachen: yields to posturing despite request to resist; mitgehen: yields to fingertip pressure (Anglepoise lamp/magnet reaction).

Catalepsy/waxy flexibility: limbs moulded into postures that are held; unlike mitmachen the arm does not return. Echo-phenomenon (catatonia, Latah, Tourette's): echopraxia = movements, echolalia = speech.
Gegenhalten: resistance proportional to applied tone; negativism: motiveless opposition to all passive movement; obstruction (Sperrung): sudden halt of a motor act.
Grimacing/schnauzkrampf, stupor (commoner in depression; paradoxically in mania), catatonic excitement, mannerisms.

Posturing: odd bizarre postures held despite efforts to move (also called catalepsy); psychological pillow: extreme posturing; stereotypies: non-goal directed (catatonia, pervasive developmental disorder, severe learning disability).

blocks.title: Stereotypy vs mannerism
rows: Behaviour has a special purpose or meaning
Wearing black goggles all the time

blocks.text: Agitation vs akathisia: psychotic agitation is very difficult to distinguish from akathisia secondary to antipsychotics, but the distinction matters because the latter requires a decrease, not an increase, in medication. Akathisia has a subjective component of restlessness together with objective evidence of unrest; at times one may have to resort to benzodiazepines when the distinction is unclear, though the dose needed may differ.

Astasia-abasia: inability to walk, sit or stand upright without obvious neurological deficit in motor strength and innervation; some patients cannot balance upright but can run with a bizarre posture. Occurs as a motor conversion disorder.

Blepharospasm is a type of focal cranial dystonia that must not be confused with catatonia; it may be seen in tardive dyskinesia. It usually begins gradually with excessive blinking, initially triggered by specific stressors (bright lights, fatigue, distress) and disappearing with sleep; concentrating on a task such as watching television often decreases the spasms. With time the spasms may become intense, functionally blinding the patient as the eyelids remain closed for longer periods.

Perseveration: the same response, verbal or motor, repeated when different stimuli (questions or instructions) are delivered. It differs from verbigeration, where repetition is spontaneous rather than in response to stimuli. Perseverative responses are goal directed (intended to answer or carry out an instruction), whereas stereotypes are not. It differs from echo phenomenon, which copies another person's responses rather than repeating one's own.

Tics are sudden involuntary (but temporarily suppressible) jerking movements, often of facial and vocal musculature but can affect any skeletal muscle group. They typically wax and wane, worsen with low mood and fatigue, and are not seen in sleep. Some appear as coordinated complex acts such as grunting or uttering syllables amounting to coprolalia (obscenities) or echophenomenon. Tics in Tourette's differ from other simple tics in being preceded by a palpable urge or prodromal sensation; tics have been conceived to share the pathophysiology of obsessions.

sections.title: 21. Miscellaneous topics: pathology of familiarity, memory and dissociation

blocks.text: Deja vu is the feeling of having seen or experienced an event that is being experienced for the first time. Its incidence decreases with age; Brown (2003) estimates ==60%== of people have experienced it. It occurs more under stress and fatigue. Reports are greater in schizophrenics and temporal lobe epileptics, suggesting temporal lobe involvement, but the duration differs: hours in schizophrenia, minutes in temporal lobe epilepsy, seconds typically.

blocks.title: Pathology of familiarity
rows: Feeling of having seen or experienced an event that is being experienced for the first time
Perception that events happening now have been lived through before
Pathological familiarity for a thought or idea
An experience that has been experienced before is not associated with feelings of familiarity; both deja vu and jamais vu can occur in normal people and in temporal lobe epilepsy

blocks.text: Some authors (Ellis, Young) include the delusional misidentification syndromes within the pathology of familiarity.

Confabulation is a falsification of memory occurring in clear consciousness, associated with organic states; suggestibility is a prominent feature. It is often described in Korsakov syndrome and may be of embarrassment or fantastic nature.

In pseudologia fantastica there is fluent plausible lying (falsification of memory) with statements that are extreme and grandiose; usually associated with dissocial or histrionic personality disorders.

In dissociative fugue there is narrowing of consciousness, wandering away from surroundings and subsequent amnesia for the episode. There is marked memory loss and loss of identity, but the patient can carry out complicated patterns of behaviour and look after himself: a gross discrepancy between memory loss and intact personality.

Ganser's syndrome (considered a hysterical dissociative disorder; the notes say there 'always seems to be an **MCQ**' on it) includes: approximate answers; clouding of consciousness with disorientation; psychogenic physical symptoms (analgesia and hyperaesthesia); pseudohallucinations (not always present); and amnesia for the abnormal behaviour.
Couvade syndrome is a sympathetic pregnancy affecting husbands (rarely other family members) during their wives' pregnancies, most frequent between 3-9 months of pregnancy.

Couvade is a conversion symptom, not delusional - the husband does not think he is pregnant. Pseudocyesis is a condition in which a woman experiences clinical signs of pregnancy without being pregnant and is convinced of the pregnancy.

Koro is a culture-bound anxiety state in which the patient believes his penis is shrinking into his abdomen and he will die as a result. It is considered a desomatisation (organ-specific depersonalisation) experience associated with folk beliefs (hence not a delusion, being culturally relevant); seen in Malaysia and Singapore.

In multiple personality disorders one-way amnesia is common (A knows B's existence, B is not aware). Possession states can occur as part of dissociation, in normal religious experiences or under hypnosis; possession states with preserved consciousness can occur in schizophrenia, while consciousness is altered in dissociative states. Lycanthropy is a form of possession in which the patient loses awareness and identity and believes he has been transformed into an animal, usually a wolf.

Out of body experiences, autoscopy, depersonalisation and transcendental experiences are often clustered in near death experiences. The neurophysiological basis of near death experience is unknown; clinical observations suggest rapid eye movement state intrusion contributes, and rapid eye movement intrusion during wakefulness is a frequent normal occurrence. A feeling of impending ego dissolution is noted in lysergic acid diethylamide intoxication.

sections.title: 22. Miscellaneous topics: depersonalisation, desomatisation, deaffectualisation and insight

blocks.text: Depersonalisation is the third most common symptom in psychiatric clinics: a change in self-awareness in which the individual feels as if he is unreal. The 'as if' quality differentiates it from psychotic states. When a similar feeling occurs for objects and the environment it is termed derealization (Mapother). It is always subjective and unpleasant, with affective change invariably and insight preserved.
Reported features: emotional numbing, loss of feelings of agency and self-esteem, disturbed body image, altered perception of time, memory and sensory experiences of all modalities.

'Depersonalisation is easily distinguished from derealisation' is the **FALSE** statement - the explanation says the two are hard to distinguish clinically, and depersonalisation is frequently accompanied by derealisation.

blocks.title: Conditions linked to depersonalisation
rows: The most common psychiatric diagnosis, followed by anxiety disorders

Depersonalisation disorder (dissociative disorder in Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition)

blocks.text: In the psychiatric population the associated affect is extremely unpleasant, unlike the normal population. Depersonalisation is often difficult to distinguish from derealization and they often occur together, the former being commoner; patients often do not report it because it is hard to express. It may be related to the pathology of familiarity (familiarity of self lost) and is associated with deja vu / jamais vu. It is frequently situational and almost always episodic. Electroconvulsive therapy can worsen depersonalisation by unknown mechanisms.

Roth described phobic anxiety depersonalisation syndrome: typically a married female in her thirties with agoraphobia and anxiety, worsening with electroconvulsive therapy; now relevant only historically.

Desomatisation is depersonalisation localised to a body part. Deaffectualisation is an extreme form of anhedonia in which not only pleasure but the capacity to feel any emotion is consistently lost; not specific to any organic syndrome, never reported in mania; patients score high on neuroticism with introversion predominant.

blocks.text: Insight is not an all-or-none phenomenon; it fluctuates within an illness for the same patient. More patients with psychoses have poor insight than those with neuroses. Loss of insight is not always related to delusions: in manic states even without delusions nearly ==50%== of patients show no insight during the acute episode, whereas schizophrenic insight loss is seen even in the chronic stage. Insight has not been consistently associated with any psychopathology of schizophrenia (some studies link it to disorganisation symptoms).

In depression insight may be higher than usual ('depressive realism'). In acute psychosis the presence of insight is associated with more self-harm and suicides. Loss of insight has been compared to anosognosia following stroke; a fronto-parietal circuit may play an important role.

Loss of insight in psychosis is phenomenologically similar to **ANOSOGNOSIA** in neurological states - it is **NOT** a trait marker (insight fluctuates) and has no consistent correlation with the domains of psychosis.

blocks.text: Frontal lobe seizures (complex partial seizures of frontal origin) are usually quite different from temporal lobe seizures: they tend to be short (less than 1 minute), occur in clusters and during sleep, and include strange automatisms such as bicycling movements, screaming or even sexual activity. A person may remain fully aware while having wild movements of the arms and legs. A frontal seizure may involve laughing (gelastic) or crying (dacrystic) as the only symptom; these are also noted in temporal lobe seizures.

Epileptic automatism is a state of clouding of consciousness occurring during or immediately after a seizure; impairment of awareness varies. The individual retains control of posture and muscle tone but performs simple or complex movements without awareness; the patient appears confused to the onlooker, with subsequent amnesia. Simple stereotyped behaviours (gesturing, grasping, lip-smacking, chewing) last a few seconds to minutes; very occasionally automatisms are prolonged (fugue states).
If automatisms are violent, they are never premeditated, seldom goal-directed and rarely involve the use of complex tools or weapons; violence is especially likely if restraining was attempted.
